pl-l3d5c1-d1e117.summary: Poses the question: since the Word assumed flesh and soul at once into unity of person, which should be granted, that a person assumed a person, a nature a nature, a person a nature, or a nature a person? And can the divine nature be called incarnate, as God and the Word are?

pl-l3d5c1-d1e120.summary: Notes that, according to the authorities, the question is partly involved and tangled and partly clear and open.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e123.summary: States what is certain: neither nature assumed person nor person assumed person, but person assumed nature.
claims: The person assumed a nature.
Neither a nature nor a person assumed a person.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e127.summary: Announces that the saints' testimonies below prove this.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e130.summary: Quotes Augustine, De fide ad Petrum: the only-begotten God took true flesh from the Virgin and preserved her virginity; he took human nature into unity of person; he took the form, i.e., the nature, of a servant into his person.
claims: God took human nature into the unity of his person.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e151.summary: Adds from the same work: God the Word took not the person of a man but the nature.
claims: The Word assumed human nature, not a human person.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e157.summary: Adds: the only-begotten Son, to cleanse man's flesh and soul, became incarnate by taking flesh and a rational soul.
claims: The Son became incarnate by assuming flesh and rational soul.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e163.summary: Concludes that these and other authorities show plainly that neither nature took person nor person person, but person took nature.
claims: The person assumed a nature.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e166.summary: Turns to the fourth part of the question, whether nature assumed nature, which is disputed among the learned: eminent doctors seem to disagree with each other and even with themselves, as the following shows.
claims: Whether nature assumed nature is disputed.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e170.summary: Quotes the Eighth Council of Toledo: only the Word was made flesh; though the whole Trinity formed the man assumed, only the Son took man into singularity of person, not into the unity of divine nature, i.e., what is proper to the Son, not what is common to the Trinity.
claims: Only the Son took man into singularity of person, not what is common to the Trinity.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e179.summary: Quotes the Eleventh Council of Toledo: Father, Son, and Spirit are of one substance, but Mary did not bear the unity of the Trinity, only the Son, who alone assumed our nature into unity of his person; the whole Trinity worked the incarnation, but only the Son took the form of a servant into singularity of person.
claims: Mary bore the Son, not the Trinity.
Only the Son took the form of a servant into singularity of person.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e185.summary: Draws the inference: these texts suggest that only the person, not the nature, assumed a nature, since if what is common to the Trinity did not take man, neither did the divine nature, which is common to the three.
claims: The councils seem to imply that the divine nature did not assume human nature.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e188.summary: Opposes Augustine, De fide ad Petrum: Christ's divinity is not alien to the Father's nature, nor his humanity to his mother's; that nature which remains always begotten from the Father took our nature without sin to be born of the Virgin.
claims: Augustine says the nature begotten of the Father assumed our nature.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e206.summary: Comments that this authority seems to teach that the divine nature assumed the human, but is troubling because it calls the nature eternally begotten of the Father, unless 'nature' is taken here for person. Otherwise the arguments of Book 1 tell against it: not nature begets nature but person begets person, since if the one nature of the Trinity begot nature, the same thing would beget itself, which Augustine denies.
claims: Nature does not beget nature.
Augustine may use 'nature' here for person.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e212.summary: Announces a clearer text showing that nature assumed nature.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e216.summary: Quotes Augustine, De Trinitate I: Christ became less than himself by taking the form of a servant, without losing the form of God in which he was equal to the Father, since the form of God took the form of a servant. Lombard infers that if the form of God took the form of a servant, nature took nature.
claims: The form of God took the form of a servant.
Therefore nature took nature.
concepts: form of God and form of a servant

pl-l3d5c1-d1e231.summary: Shows that 'form' means nature, quoting Augustine, De fide ad Petrum: when Christ is said to be in the form of God, the fullness of nature is to be understood, since he was always in the nature of God the Father from whom he was born.
claims: 'Form' signifies nature.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e243.summary: Adds Hilary, De Trinitate XII: to be in the form of God means nothing other than to remain in God's nature.
claims: To be in the form of God is to remain in God's nature.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e255.summary: Concludes: since 'form' means nature and the form of God took the form of a servant, the divine nature took the human nature.
claims: The divine nature took human nature.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e258.summary: Adds Jerome's Explanation of the faith: the Son of God suffered truly, not in appearance, according to the substance assumed, not the substance that assumed. From this it is clear that the divine substance assumed the human.
claims: Christ suffered according to the assumed substance.
The divine substance assumed the human substance.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e270.summary: Notes that Augustine's words quoted earlier suggest both that the Word alone was made flesh and took human nature, and that the divine nature took it: the Trinity made the Word alone flesh, in which divine and human nature remain unchanged, and the supreme divinity bears the humanity united to it.
claims: Augustine says both that the Word alone was made flesh and that humanity is united to divinity.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e280.summary: Recalls that the same author also said the servile form, which the whole Trinity made, was assumed by the Son alone.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e286.summary: Observes how diverse the authorities are on this question, giving later readers occasion for various and contrary opinions.
claims: The authorities on this question are diverse.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e289.summary: Gives Lombard's resolution, seeking to exclude falsehood and contradiction from Scripture and agreeing with the orthodox fathers: the Son's person assumed human nature, and the divine nature, united to human nature in the Son, united or assumed it to itself, so it is truly called incarnate. 'Only the Son took the form of a servant' excludes the Father and Spirit, not the divine nature. 'What is proper to the Son, not what is common to the Trinity' means the divine nature united human nature to itself properly in the Son's hypostasis, not in all three persons in common.
claims: The person of the Son assumed human nature.
The divine nature united human nature to itself in the Son's person.
The divine nature is truly incarnate.
'Only the Son' excludes the other persons, not the divine nature.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e295.summary: Confirms this reading with John Damascene: in the Word's incarnation the whole and perfect divine nature was incarnate in one of its hypostases, united to human nature, not part to part; the whole divine nature was united to the whole human nature.
claims: The whole divine nature was incarnate in one hypostasis.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e304.summary: Adds Damascene: the same nature is in each hypostasis; when we say, with Athanasius and Cyril, that the nature of the Word is incarnate, we mean the deity is united to flesh, one incarnate nature of God the Word; the Word possesses both what is common to the substance and what is proper to the hypostasis.
claims: The Word has both what is common to the divine substance and what is proper to his hypostasis.

pl-l3d5c1-d1e316.summary: Concludes that the divine nature was incarnate and so is truly said to have assumed human nature.
claims: The divine nature was incarnate and assumed human nature.

pl-l3d5c1.summary: Asks which formula is correct: whether a person assumed a person, a nature a nature, a person a nature, or a nature a person, and whether the divine nature may be called incarnate. It is certain that the person assumed a nature and that neither a nature nor a person assumed a person (Augustine, De fide ad Petrum). Whether nature assumed nature is disputed: Toledo VIII and XI say only the Son took man into singularity of person, not what is common to the Trinity, implying it did not. But Augustine says the nature born of the Father assumed ours, and that the form of God took the form of a servant, where form means nature (Augustine, Hilary); Jerome says the divine substance assumed the human. Lombard harmonizes: the Son's person assumed human nature, and the divine nature united human nature to itself in the Son's person, not in all three. So the divine nature is truly incarnate, as Damascene, citing Athanasius and Cyril, confirms.
claims: The person of the Word assumed a nature, not a person.
Neither nature nor person assumed a person.
The divine nature assumed human nature in the person of the Son.
The divine nature is truly called incarnate.
'Only the Son assumed' excludes the other persons, not the divine nature.
concepts: form of God and form of a servant
